name: Thematic Coding
title: Thematic Coding
answer: Thematic coding is a qualitative analysis method for finding, naming and organising patterns of meaning across a body of text, interview transcripts, field notes, open survey answers or documents. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where it usually feeds a later stage such as theory building, instrument design or a quantitative strand. The unit of work is the code, a short label attached to a passage, and the theme, a grouping of codes that answers the research question. It differs from counting words because the analyst interprets meaning rather than only tallying occurrences.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Thematic coding is a qualitative analysis method for finding, naming and organising patterns of meaning across a body of text, interview transcripts, field notes, open survey answers or documents. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where it usually feeds a later stage such as theory building, instrument design or a quantitative strand. The unit of work is the code, a short label attached to a passage, and the theme, a grouping of codes that answers the research question. It differs from counting words because the analyst interprets meaning rather than only tallying occurrences.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a corpus of textual material plus a coding environment, which may be a spreadsheet, a qualitative data analysis package such as NVivo or ATLAS.ti, or a general tool the team already uses. Transcripts arrive from interviews, focus groups, open-ended survey items, documents or public records, and they need cleaning, anonymising and consistent formatting before coding starts. A codebook or code list is the shared artefact, holding code names, definitions and example excerpts. In mixed methods designs the coded output is often exported as counts or categories for joining to survey or outcome data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Coding usually proceeds in passes, starting with familiarisation and open coding of a subset, then refining codes into a stable scheme, then applying that scheme across the full corpus. Two or more coders may code the same passages independently so agreement can be checked, and disagreements are resolved by discussion or by revising the definitions. Themes are built by clustering related codes, testing them against negative cases and writing memos that record analytic decisions. Reporting quotes excerpts as evidence and states how many participants or documents support each theme, and reflexivity notes record how the analyst's position shaped the reading.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are loss of context when a code is applied too broadly, drift between coders when definitions are vague, and overclaiming frequency as if it measured importance. Provenance matters, so each theme should trace back to specific excerpts and each excerpt to its source document, with the version of the codebook recorded. Consent, confidentiality and data protection rules govern storage and quoting, and identifying details are removed or masked before sharing. Where automated coding or topic modelling is used, it is treated as a first pass that a human reviews, and the tool and settings are documented rather than presented as the analyst.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward hybrid workflows, where language models propose candidate codes or cluster passages while researchers keep the interpretive decisions and the audit trail. That raises practical questions about reproducibility, since a model-assisted coding run may not repeat exactly, and about disclosure, since readers increasingly expect to know when software shaped a codebook. Shared codebooks, open coding frameworks and archived excerpts are becoming more common as journals and funders ask for evidence behind qualitative claims. The method itself is unlikely to be replaced, because the judgement about what a passage means and why it matters remains the analyst's work.
